parts: I'm starting a side project called Lantern. It's a home energy dashboard that reads my smart meter (an Octopus Home Mini) every 30 seconds and shows usage, cost and a forecast for the day. I want to store readings for at least two years. What should the storage look like? My email for the Octopus API is mo.example@example.com and my API key is 9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0 in case that matters.

Congratulations on Lantern. First, please rotate that API key: you pasted it into a chat, which should be treated as a leak.

For storage you are looking at roughly 1 million readings a year at 30-second resolution, which is small. Two sensible options:

1. PostgreSQL with the TimescaleDB extension. Familiar SQL, automatic partitioning by time, built-in continuous aggregates for hourly and daily rollups, and compression that will shrink two years of readings to a few hundred megabytes.
2. InfluxDB. Purpose built for time series, very fast ingest, but a second query language to learn and a weaker story for joining with relational data like tariffs.

Given you will want to join readings against tariff tables and you already know SQL, I would lean towards Postgres with Timescale.

Postgres with Timescale it is. I'm assuming the Home Mini keeps giving 30-second data for free and that my Raspberry Pi 4 can run Postgres comfortably. Siyu (a friend from Beijing, she's a lawyer who tinkers with home automation on weekends) suggested Grafana for the dashboard rather than building my own UI. Thoughts?

Both assumptions are worth checking rather than trusting. Octopus has changed the Home Mini API before, and a Pi 4 with 4 GB runs Postgres fine but Timescale compression jobs can spike memory, so set shared_buffers conservatively.

Siyu's suggestion is a good one. Grafana talks to Postgres natively, gives you time-range pickers, alerting and annotations for free, and you can always build a custom UI later if the dashboard outgrows it. Start with Grafana.
Agreed, Grafana for now. Open question I don't have an answer to yet: how do I downsample two years of 30-second data for the graphs without losing the peaks? I'll come back to that.
Back to Lantern. I want to understand time-series downsampling properly. If I average 30-second readings into 5-minute buckets, the kettle spike disappears. What do people do?

The standard trick is to keep more than one statistic per bucket. For each 5-minute bucket store the mean, the max and the min. Graph the mean as a line and the max as a faint band above it, so peaks stay visible. Timescale continuous aggregates can maintain these buckets automatically as new readings arrive.

For very long ranges you can also use the LTTB algorithm (largest triangle three buckets), which picks the visually important points rather than averaging. Grafana has a plugin for it, and Timescale ships an lttb() function in the toolkit extension.

That answers my open question from last week. I'll do mean plus max plus min in a continuous aggregate at 5 minutes, and a second one at 1 hour. Siyu also mentioned that her law firm's IT team uses Grafana annotations to mark deploys; I could mark tariff changes the same way.
That is a clean design. Two aggregates, refreshed on a schedule, and raw data compressed after seven days. Annotations for tariff changes will make the cost graph much easier to read.

Decision time for Lantern. Keep everything on the Raspberry Pi 4 at home, or move Postgres and Grafana to a small VPS? The Pi has been fine so far but my broadband dropped twice this week and I lost readings.

The readings are lost because the collector and the database are on the same box behind a flaky connection. You have three options:

1. Stay on the Pi and add a local buffer so the collector retries when the meter API is unreachable. Cheapest, but the dashboard is unavailable when your broadband is down.
2. Move Postgres and Grafana to a VPS and keep only the collector on the Pi. The dashboard stays up, but readings still stop while the Pi cannot reach the meter API, and you pay a few pounds a month.
3. Move everything to the VPS and poll the Octopus API from there. Simplest operationally, but you depend entirely on the cloud API rather than the local Home Mini feed.

If the two outages were broadband rather than power, option 2 gives you the most resilience for the least change.

Going with option 2: Postgres and Grafana on a VPS, collector stays on the Pi with a local retry buffer. Assumptions: a small VPS is under 5 pounds a month and the Pi collector can buffer a day of readings on its SD card. I'll revisit in June if the bill or the SD card wear becomes a problem.

Noted. Two things to check by June: the actual VPS invoice, and SD card health, since a day of 30-second readings is only about 3,000 rows and will not wear the card, but Postgres write-ahead logs would have. Moving the database off the Pi removes that risk.
